2:40 · 30 min

Concept + hand calculation

Regular expressions

A small language for describing patterns in text

Why start here?

Regexes are everywhere

  • form validation (email, PAN, GSTIN)
  • invoice and log parsing
  • redacting personal data (PII)
  • the first step of every NLP pipeline
  • ELIZA (1966), the first chatbot, was built from patterns

Regular expressions are

  • deterministic: the same input gives the same output
  • auditable: you can read the rule
  • cheap: 30,000 rows in under a second
  • no training data needed

Building blocks 1: what to match

Pattern Means Matches
filter literal text "water filter"
[Ff]ilter one of these characters "Filter", "filter"
[0-9] a range any single digit
[^0-9] anything except any non-digit
\d \w \s digit · word char · space \d = [0-9]
. any character "a", "7", "$", …
\$ \. escape special characters a real "$" or "."

Building blocks 2: how many, and where

Quantifier Means
? 0 or 1 (optional)
* 0 or more
+ 1 or more
{3} exactly 3
{2,5} 2 to 5
Anchor Means
^ start of string
$ end of string
\b word boundary

colou?r → "color", "colour"  ·  \d{6} → "576104"  ·  \bloud\b → "loud" but not "cloudy"

Building blocks 3: choices and groups

Pattern Means
noise|noisy|loud alternation: any one of these
(month|year)s? capturing group: remember what matched
(?:month|year)s? non-capturing group: group only
(?i) ignore case
.* vs .*? greedy (longest) vs lazy (shortest) 
"<b>Great</b> price <b>fast</b>"
<b>.*</b>    →  <b>Great</b> price <b>fast</b>   (greedy)
<b>.*?</b>   →  <b>Great</b>                      (lazy)

Worked example: find prices

Test sentence: Paid $24.99 here, Sears wanted $1,299 for the unit

Attempt Pattern Result
1 $\d+ nothing: $ means "end of string"
2 \$\d+ $24, $1: cut short
3 \$\d+(?:\.\d\d)? $24.99 ✓  $1 ✗
4 \$\d{1,3}(?:,\d{3})*(?:\.\d\d)? $24.99 ✓  $1,299 ✓

This is how regexes work in practice: write a pattern → test it → read the misses → refine it.

✏️ On paper, 4 minutes

Which of these does \b[6-9]\d{9}\b match?

  1. 9822967803
  2. 4587120936
  3. SN9822967803
  1. 98229 67803
  2. +919822967803
  3. Call 7019283746.

Answer: (a) and (f). (b) starts with 4. (c) has no word boundary between N and 9. (d) the space breaks \d{9}. (e) is the trickiest: 1 and 9 are both word characters, so there is no \b between them.

Two ways a pattern can be wrong

False positive (FP): a wrong match

loud also matches "cloudy water"

Fix it by making the pattern stricter, which raises precision.

False negative (FN): a miss

[A-Z]{2,}\d{3,} misses "K200"

Fix it by making the pattern looser, which raises recall.

A correct match is a true positive (TP).

\[ \text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP+FP} \qquad \text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP+FN} \qquad F_1 = \frac{2PR}{P+R} \]

✏️ On paper, 3 minutes

Your "noise complaint" pattern flags 50 reviews. On checking, 40 of them really are noise complaints. The dataset contains 80 noise complaints in total.

Precision? Recall? F1?

\[ P = \tfrac{40}{50} = 0.80 \qquad R = \tfrac{40}{80} = 0.50 \qquad F_1 = \tfrac{2(0.8)(0.5)}{1.3} \approx 0.62 \]

So what: it is precise but misses half of the complaints. A dashboard built on it would understate the noise problem by 2×.

Manager's lens: which error costs more?

Use case Worse error So favour
Redacting phone numbers before sharing data a missed phone (FN): a leak recall
Auto-closing tickets marked "resolved" closing an open ticket (FP) precision
A "noise complaints" dashboard tile depends on who reads it ask them

There is no "correct" regex, only one that fits the purpose.

From paper to Python

import re
re.findall(r"\$\d+(?:\.\d\d)?", text)        # list of matches
re.search(r"after (\d+) (month|year)", text)  # first match + groups
re.sub(r"<br\s*/?>", " ", text)                # replace

# same thing on a whole pandas column
reviews["text"].str.contains(r"\bloud\b", case=False)   # flag
reviews["text"].str.extract(r"after (\d+) (month|year)")  # → columns

⚠️ Always use raw strings, r"…". ⚠️ With a capturing group, findall returns only the group.

Ethics check 🛑

India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 treats names, phones and emails as personal data. Organisations must protect them and use them only for the purpose they were collected for.

  1. A redactor with 98% recall runs on 1 million tickets a year. How many phone numbers leak?
  2. Who decides what error rate is acceptable: the analyst, legal, or the customer?
  3. The vendor sends the redacted tickets to an LLM API. What could still identify a customer?

Q1: roughly 20,000 leaks if every ticket has a phone number. Q3: order IDs plus addresses, names in the body text, unusual complaints, city with PIN. Point: regex redaction is necessary but not sufficient.

Where regexes stop working

"Great, it broke after 2 days 🙄"

Sarcasm: a pattern can't read tone → W4 sentiment

"filter" · "cartridge" · "purifier insert"

Synonyms: same meaning, different strings → W5–6 vectors

"Khan Traders", "Mr. Pai from Udupi"

Names have no fixed shape → learned models, W9

50 intents, messy language

Hand rules don't scale → learn the rules from data
